description:
George is a senior software engineer. He builds data pipelines and geospatial tools. Christina is a product designer. She designs consumer mobile apps. We live in Athens, Greece.

Our challenge is the Lunar Landing Site Navigator. We will build a tool that compares Moon landing sites and dates in seconds. The tool shows three things:

The positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the horizon

The duration of sunlight

The times when direct communication with Earth is possible
summary: Lunalyze answers one question for lunar mission planners: which south-pole landing site, and which week? You can pick up to three sites (or type coordinates), a landing date and how long the mission stays. For each site, Lunalyze works out where the Sun and Earth are against that site's real horizon, built from NASA LRO LOLA terrain maps, so the hills that hide them are counted. It shows how much of the stay is in sunlight (solar power), how much has Earth in view (direct radio contact), and the longest stretch with neither. Each site ends in a plain verdict, "Fits your mission" or "Risky", with a one-line reason, and the best site comes first. This matters because Artemis crews and robotic landers live on sunlight and on talking to Earth, and at the south pole both come and go behind terrain. Sun and Earth positions are checked against NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.01°. The whole setup lives in the URL, so a shared link reopens the same comparison. We aimed to use plain words come first, so teachers and the public can follow along too.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunalyze is a decision-support tool for picking a lunar south-pole landing site and date. You choose up to 3 places (13 known sites such as Artemis candidate regions, Malapert, Haworth, Nobile, IM-1/IM-2, or your own coordinates), a landing date and time in UTC, how flexible the date is, and how long the mission stays (½ to 3 Moon days). Lunalyze then compares the sites side by side.

HOW IT WORKS

- Terrain: we built a 360° horizon mask for each site from NASA LRO LOLA polar elevation maps (240 m, 80 m and 20 m). The mask records how high the terrain rises in every direction.

- Sky: Sun and Earth positions come from astronomy-engine. An automated test checks 16 values against NASA JPL Horizons, and they must agree to within 0.01°.

- Result: comparing the Sun and Earth against the mask gives, for every hour of the stay, whether the site has sunlight and whether Earth is in view.

- Verdict: a site "Fits your mission" if it never goes more than 50 hours without both the Sun and Earth. Otherwise it is "Risky", with the exact dates. Sites are ranked by fit, then by the shortest dark gap, then sunlight, then Earth time.

- Our mask method is checked against NASA's PGDA 69 average illumination maps.

WHAT YOU SEE

A verdict per site, a horizon strip showing the Sun and Earth against the hills, sunlight and Earth-in-view meters, countdowns ("Sunset in…"), a timeline, a south-pole map and a 3D terrain view. The whole scenario is in the URL, so a link can be shared.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Artemis and commercial landers depend on solar power and on direct contact with Earth. At the south pole, the Sun stays near the horizon and hills block it for hours or days at a time. Lunalyze turns raw terrain data into a plain answer a planner can act on and a teacher can explain.

HONEST DATA

Every number on screen comes from the calculation code; the visuals never invent numbers. Each number shows its unit and time range. Sites without full terrain coverage are marked with a caveat.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React 19, TanStack Query, Zustand, three.js / react-three-fiber, Vite, Vitest, Python + NumPy (terrain pipeline), GitHub Actions, Vercel.

CREATIVITY AND DESIGN CHOICES

We built a comparison tool, not just a Moon viewer, because the real question is "which one, and when?". We use plain words ("Time in sunlight", not "illumination fraction"). The app follows WCAG 2.1 AA: colour is never the only signal, hidden things are drawn dashed and visible ones solid, and every control works from the keyboard.
